newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.Africa mine wins approval to sell own gold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Africa mine wins approval to sell own gold.

text.p: South Africa eased state control of gold marketing on Thursday, allowing Harmony Gold Mining Co Ltd to become the first mine to be allowed to sell a portion of its own production.
Harmony said it had received approval from the central Reserve Bank to market internationally a third of its gold production, amounting to eight tonnes a year.
This is the first time a South African producer has been allowed to sell its gold directly to the world, rather than via the central bank.

Harmony is part of the Randgold and Exploration Co Ltd group and commercial director Brett Kebble said the company's other mines were likely to follow suit in establishing similar small mine-based refineries.
Harmony said permission had been granted with immediate effect but it would only start selling gold independently when its existing refining agreement with Rand Refinery ends in October this year.
At present all South Africa's mines refine their gold at the Rand Refinery -- the world's biggest -- which is collectively owned by the industry.
But Harmony announced last year that it planned to break ranks by establishing its own commercial-scale gold refinery, which should be completed in the third quarter of 1997.

"It's clear it is going to be possible to market gold direct and it might be possible to achieve a higher price than is obtained through the Reserve Bank, so it must have merit on the that basis," Kebble told Reuters.
Randgold calculates that it will be cheaper to refine its own gold than using the Rand Refinery.

It says the cost of establishing the Harmony plant and acquiring new technology will be 3.3 million rand ($710,000) which is less than the annual savings it expects to achieve by smelting and refining its own gold.

Harmony managing director Bernard Swanepoel welcomed the partial exchange control exemption granted by the Reserve Bank but said he hoped that Harmony would eventually be allowed to market its full production of around 24 tonnes a year.
"At least we are now in a position to finalise negotiations with potential international partners regarding the eight tonnes of gold per year which the Reserve Bank has put at our disposal," he said.
Options under consideration include marketing gold bullion in the form of kilogram bars as well as the establishment of a local gold jewellery manufacturing business.
Randgold mines in total produce around 50 tonnes of gold a year, or 10 percent of national output.
South Africa is the world's biggest gold-producing country, producing 522.4 tonnes in 1994, or 23 percent of global output.
